title: Christa Pike's injuries from botched execution still unknown, lawyers say
summary: The lawyers for convicted murderer Christa Pike say the full extent of the injuries she suffered from her botched execution are still unknown and that she needs to be examined by medical experts,…

image.caption: Christa Pike, seen here in a 2023 Tennessee Department of Correction booking photograph, survived an attempted exectution in September. (Tennessee Department of Correction/Handout via REUTERS)

blocks.text: The lawyers for convicted murderer Christa Pike say the full extent of the injuries she suffered from her botched execution are still unknown and that she needs to be examined by medical experts, according to a report.
Lawyer calls for examination by 2 clinical psychologists
Pike's attorney asked a judge on Monday to order Tennessee's Department of Corrections to allow medical experts retained by her legal team to evaluate Pike without her counsel present, CNN reported.
Pike's legal team reportedly wants two clinical psychologists — one with "specialties in complex trauma" and another with "expertise in torture and trauma" — to examine her.
In a statement last month, Pike, 50, said that while she continues to get stronger, she has been in pain since surviving the execution attempt in September.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts," she said.
"I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

Pike survived two doses of the drug pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death in the U.S.
The slaying involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir.
The execution attempt initially left Pike unconscious and on a ventilator, with severe arm injuries. She was hospitalized but has since returned to the prison where she was serving her sentence.
Pike is the first person known to have survived being injected with a full dose of execution drugs.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," Pike said in her statement.
Pike's attorneys have urged Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to reduce Pike's sentence to life imprisonment. But Lee has said he suspects her sentence will remain unless determined otherwise by the courts.

items: Pike in 'constant pain' since surviving execution attempt

blocks.text: Following the unsuccessful execution attempt, Lee halted further executions for the remainder of the year and ordered a comprehensive third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.
Meanwhile, a Tennessee judge has ordered that all evidence from the attempted execution be preserved so a full investigation can take place.
